opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I treated it less like watching videos and more like doing a lab course. Karpathy's "Neural Networks: Zero to Hero" series is structured so that you build everything from the ground up, so I tried to follow that spirit very strictly.

I started with micrograd, the tiny autograd engine. That one was really important for me, because before that, backpropagation was something I understood mathematically but had never felt with my hands. Writing the `Value` class, implementing the backward pass for each operation, and then watching a small neural net actually train on top of something I wrote myself made the chain rule concrete in a way no textbook had.

Then I moved on to makemore. You go from a bigram model to an MLP, then batch norm, then a WaveNet-like architecture. I think people sometimes skip those middle videos to jump straight to the GPT one, but for me they were the most valuable. In the batch norm episode he does the "become a backprop ninja" exercise, where you manually derive the gradients through cross-entropy, batch norm, and the linear layers, tensor by tensor. It's painful, it took me a few evenings, but after that I could look at a training loss curve or activation statistics and actually have an intuition about what was going wrong.

By the time I got to "Let's build GPT," the transformer didn't feel like magic anymore. Self-attention is basically a weighted aggregation where the weights depend on the data, and he builds it up step by step, starting from a simple average over previous tokens with a lower-triangular mask, then making it data-dependent with queries and keys. Once you see it that way, multi-head attention, residual connections, and layer norm all feel like natural engineering decisions rather than arbitrary choices from a paper.

My main method was: watch a section, pause, close the video, and try to write the code myself from memory. When I got stuck, I'd go back, but only for the specific part I was stuck on. I also kept a notebook where I wrote down every "wait, why?" moment, like why we scale by the square root of the head dimension, or why the residual stream matters so much for optimization, and I'd come back and try to answer those myself.

After that I did the tokenizer video and reproduced GPT-2 with nanoGPT, which taught me a lot about the practical side: mixed precision, gradient accumulation, learning rate schedules, and how much of real-world training is about engineering details rather than the architecture itself.

So I'd say the biggest lesson was that understanding comes from rebuilding, not from reading. Karpathy is very good at making you feel that nothing is too complicated if you build it one line at a time.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes rebuilding code and studying Karpathy’s video series, but does not say Su Tinghao challenged himself to read one research paper per day.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't start with the theory. I started by just typing along. Karpathy's whole series is built on this idea that you should write every line yourself, so the first thing I did was open a blank notebook, put his video on one monitor, and refuse to copy-paste anything. If he wrote a function, I wrote it. If he made a typo and debugged it on camera, I let myself make my own mistakes and debug them too. That slowness turned out to be the point.

The thing I appreciated most was the order he teaches things in. He doesn't begin with "here is a transformer." He begins with micrograd, which is basically a tiny autograd engine, just scalars and a backward pass. Then makemore, where you're predicting the next character in a name. Then a bigram model, then an MLP, and only after all of that does attention show up. By the time you reach the attention block, it feels almost inevitable. You've already hit the wall of "my model can't see far enough back in the sequence," so attention arrives as the answer to a problem you've personally felt, not as a formula someone handed you.

My own rule was that after each video, I would close the notebook and try to rebuild the same thing from memory the next morning. The first few times I got embarrassingly stuck. I remember being unable to explain to myself why we divide by the square root of the head dimension in the attention scores. So I went back, re-derived it, and watched what happened to the softmax when I removed it. Seeing the attention weights collapse into near one-hot vectors made it click in a way reading the paper never did.

The other thing I'd say is that I didn't try to make it big. I trained on tiny Shakespeare on a laptop, watched the loss go from gibberish to something that looked vaguely Elizabethan, and that was enough. The goal wasn't a good model. The goal was to have no magic left in the stack. Once I could draw the whole data flow from token embedding to logits on a whiteboard without looking, I felt like I actually understood it, and that's when reading the GPT-2 and GPT-3 papers finally became easy rather than intimidating.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes learning through Karpathy’s videos and rebuilding models from memory, but does not say Su set himself a challenge to read one research paper per day.

astra-6.text: I approached it as a coding exercise rather than just watching lectures. I’d watch a section, pause, and try to implement that piece myself. Then I’d go back when I got stuck or couldn’t explain why something worked. With the transformer, I tried to follow how the data moved through the model—what the tensor shapes were, what attention was doing, and how the prediction turned into a loss. The goal was to get a small version working and understand each part well enough that I could change it, rather than simply reproduce the code.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes implementing a GPT and transformer while following the video series; it does not mention a daily research-paper reading challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I approached it as a build-along rather than just watching lectures. I’d watch a section, pause, and try to implement it myself. If something worked but I couldn’t explain why, I’d go back and work through it again.

The biggest thing was connecting the concepts to the code. With attention, for example, I wanted to understand what each operation was doing and how the dimensions fit together, rather than just copying it. Then I’d make small changes and see what happened.

My goal wasn’t to reproduce the whole thing as quickly as possible. It was to get to the point where I could explain the pieces and rebuild them on my own.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning by implementing Karpathy’s material, but does not say Su Tinghao challenged himself to read one research paper per day.
